CAR BUYING KNOWLEDGE CENTRE · USED CAR BUYING

How to Read a Report in Canada

Six key sections to review before you buy a used vehicle — plus the questions worth asking.

Practical Canadian Buyer Guide

What is a CARFAX Canada report?

A CARFAX Canada Vehicle History Report brings together available records from participating sources. It can help you review accidents, registration, service visits, odometer readings, previous use and other history before buying.

Important to know: A clean report does not guarantee the vehicle has never been in an accident. A standard Vehicle History Report does not include a Canadian lien check; verify liens separately or purchase the appropriate lien-check product.

Six key sections to review

Here's what each section means, what to look for and the key questions to ask.

01

Vehicle identity & registration

Check the VIN, model year, make, registration history and vehicle branding. Match the VIN on the report to the car and its documents.

Buyer questionDoes the VIN match everywhere? Is there an unexplained registration or branding change?
02

Accident & damage history

Review reported collision dates, damage descriptions and repair estimates. Ask for photos and invoices to understand the actual repairs.

Buyer questionWas there structural, flood or airbag damage? Can I see repair documentation?
03

Service & maintenance records

Look for dated maintenance entries and major repairs. Missing records do not necessarily mean the vehicle was neglected.

Buyer questionAre the service records consistent? Were major maintenance items completed?
04

Odometer (mileage) records

Compare recorded kilometres across dates. Check for unexpected decreases or readings inconsistent with the vehicle's age.

Buyer questionDo the recorded kilometres make sense compared with the dashboard and service records?
05

Previous owners

Review available ownership and registration history. Multiple owners are not automatically a problem, but frequent changes deserve questions.

Buyer questionWhy did ownership change? Are there unexplained short ownership periods?
06

Vehicle use & lien information

Look for available rental, fleet, taxi or commercial-use indicators. A standard Vehicle History Report does not include a Canadian lien check.

Buyer questionHow was the vehicle used, and has a separate lien search been completed?
BEYOND THE BASICS

Real-world CARFAX examples: what to do next

The six cards above are your quick reference. These deeper examples show how to interpret a record, what it does not prove, and the next step to take before buying.

01

Vehicle identity, registration & branding

A vehicle history report starts with the identity of the vehicle—not the accident section. Confirm that the VIN on the report matches the VIN visible through the windshield, the driver-door label and the registration documents. Check the make, model, model year and provinces of registration. A mismatch may be a typo, but it must be resolved before money changes hands.

Example

A seller advertises a 2021 SUV, but the report identifies a different model year or the VIN on the dashboard differs by one character. Do not assume the paperwork is simply outdated. Ask the seller to correct the discrepancy and independently verify the vehicle's identity.

How to interpret it

Look for branding such as normal, salvage, rebuilt or irreparable, where reported. Branding rules and terminology vary by province. A rebuilt designation can affect insurance, financing, value and resale. Do not treat a clean-looking exterior as proof that the vehicle has a normal history.

What the buyer should do

Photograph the VIN plates; compare the report, registration and bill of sale; ask about provincial moves and branding changes. If a mismatch remains unexplained, pause the purchase.

02

Accident & damage history

A report may list a collision, an insurance claim, a damage estimate, a repair record or a police-reported incident. These are not interchangeable. Review the date, event description, location and available dollar amounts. Some repairs and incidents may never appear because not every source reports data.

Example

A report shows an $8,000 damage estimate. That number alone cannot tell you whether the vehicle suffered structural damage. Parts, labour and sensor calibration can be costly, while some serious damage may be repaired outside an insurance claim. Request invoices, photos and the repair facility's details.

How to interpret it

Look for repeated collisions, airbag deployment, flood or fire history, major structural repairs and unexplained gaps in the seller's explanation. A report stating 'no accidents reported' means none were found in the available records—not that the vehicle is guaranteed accident-free.

What the buyer should do

Have an independent mechanic or qualified body shop inspect previous repairs, structural areas and safety systems. Ask for documentation and walk away if the seller refuses reasonable verification.

03

Service & maintenance records

Service entries can show when and where work was recorded, but a history report is not a complete maintenance log. Some independent shops, home mechanics and dealerships may not send records. Read dates and kilometres together to build a timeline, and compare it with the manufacturer's maintenance schedule.

Example

A five-year-old vehicle shows only two service entries. This is a reason to ask for more evidence, not proof that oil changes were skipped. The owner may have invoices, receipts, an app-based service history or maintenance records from a shop that did not contribute data.

How to interpret it

Watch for repeated repairs to the same system, long unexplained gaps and signs that major scheduled maintenance may be overdue. On higher-mileage vehicles, ask about brakes, tires, transmission service and other model-specific items.

What the buyer should do

Request dated invoices, compare kilometres with the odometer and budget for overdue maintenance. Use an independent pre-purchase inspection to assess the car's current condition.

04

Odometer readings & timeline

A report may show kilometre readings from service, registration, inspections or other recorded events. Put the readings in date order. Normally the figure should rise as the vehicle is driven, though clerical mistakes and unit conversions can occur. Missing readings alone do not prove odometer tampering.

Example

An entry shows 85,000 km in 2022 and 62,000 km in 2024. This is an inconsistency worth investigating. It might be a data-entry error, an instrument-cluster replacement or something more serious. The report by itself does not establish which explanation is correct.

How to interpret it

Compare the current dashboard reading with the newest report entry, maintenance receipts and provincial records where available. Very low kilometres for an older vehicle are not automatically suspicious, but the story should be consistent.

What the buyer should do

Ask the seller for supporting records and a written explanation of any decrease or mismatch. If the discrepancy cannot be resolved, do not rely on the advertised mileage.

05

Previous owners & vehicle use

Ownership and registration information can help explain how the car was used and how often it changed hands. Availability varies, and a change in registration does not always mean a new retail owner. A move between provinces or a transfer within a family can produce entries that need context.

Example

A three-year-old car appears to have changed owners three times. That is a question to investigate, not an automatic rejection. Ask about the length of each ownership period and whether transfers involved a dealer, a lease return or a personal sale.

How to interpret it

Look for indications of rental, fleet, taxi or commercial use where available. Such use is not automatically disqualifying; condition, maintenance and price matter. A well-maintained fleet vehicle may be preferable to a neglected personal-use car.

What the buyer should do

Ask how the car was used, request maintenance evidence, and compare its condition and price with similar vehicles. Arrange an inspection regardless of the ownership count.

06

Liens, recalls & report limitations

A lien is a legal claim that may arise when a vehicle is used as security for a debt. Do not assume the seller owns the car free and clear simply because a history report looks clean. CARFAX Canada offers different report products; the standard Vehicle History Report does not include a Canadian lien check. Confirm which product or separate search you are relying on.

Example

A private seller still owes money on the car. Even if the car drives perfectly and the accident section is clear, the buyer needs a safe process to discharge the lien and document the release. A verbal promise to pay the loan later is not enough protection.

How to interpret it

Check open recalls through the manufacturer using the VIN, and ask whether required repairs were completed. Remember that report information depends on available participating sources and may be incomplete or delayed. Provincial registry requirements and lien-search coverage can vary.

What the buyer should do

Complete an appropriate Canadian lien search, verify any discharge directly with the lender or registry as applicable, check recalls and have the vehicle independently inspected before finalizing the deal.

When should you slow down—or walk away?

Keep checking

Minor or unclear entries with a reasonable explanation and supporting records.

Investigate further

Large or repeated claims, unexplained mileage changes, incomplete maintenance evidence or frequent ownership changes.

Pause the deal

VIN mismatch, unresolved lien, undisclosed branding, refused inspection or documentation that contradicts the seller's story.

These are practical warning signs, not automatic legal or mechanical conclusions. A qualified inspection and appropriate registry checks remain important.
